```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

The distinction between one-step and three-step approaches concerns whether
external variables are allowed to influence the estimation and definition of
latent profiles. External variables are not included among the indicators
used to identify the profiles but are introduced to examine their
relationships with profile membership. These variables may function as
predictors of profile membership, covariates, or distal outcomes.

In the three-step approach, the measurement model is estimated first, using
only the indicators specified to define the profiles. Once the profiles have
been identified, individuals are assigned to their most likely profile based
on their posterior membership probabilities. In the subsequent step, external
variables are incorporated into the analysis while correcting for the
classification errors associated with this assignment. This correction is
important because profile membership is latent and individuals cannot
necessarily be classified with complete certainty. By accounting for this
uncertainty, the three-step approach reduces the bias that would arise from
treating assigned profile membership as if it were directly observed.
Importantly, the original measurement model remains unchanged: the
profile-specific means and other measurement parameters are not re-estimated
in response to the external variables.

In contrast, the one-step approach incorporates external variables directly
into the latent profile model, estimating the measurement and structural
components simultaneously. Consequently, the external variables can influence
the estimation of profile membership and, depending on the model
specification, alter the profile characteristics and classification of
individuals. Although this approach allows the relationships between latent
profiles and external variables to be estimated jointly, it may produce a
different profile solution from the model estimated using only the original
measurement indicators (Bolck et al., 2004; Vermunt, 2010).

This distinction is particularly relevant in person-centred research, where
profiles are interpreted as substantively meaningful subgroups characterized
by distinct patterns across a set of indicators (Saqr et al., 2024; Scrucca
et al., 2024). Researchers often seek to investigate the characteristics,
antecedents, and consequences of these subgroups after establishing their
measurement structure. In such cases, allowing external variables to
influence profile estimation may change the very subgroups that the
subsequent analyses are intended to investigate. The three-step approach
addresses this concern by preserving the original profile solution while
accounting for classification uncertainty. Staged estimation extends the same
principle to group classes in multilevel models, keeping the profile solution fixed while the group classes are estimated. Thus, three-step methods are particularly useful when the
objective is to investigate relationships with external variables without
changing the substantive meaning of the previously identified profiles.

This guide demonstrates these approaches in a two-level latent profile model
of course engagement, in which course enrolments are nested within students.
The measurement model is first estimated from the engagement indicators
alone, and its classification-error matrix is examined, since this matrix is
the basis of every three-step correction. The previous grade before each enrolment
is then related to the profiles in three ways: as a distal variable whose mean
is compared across profiles with `three_step()`, using the BCH and maximum
likelihood corrections and, for comparison, uncorrected modal assignment; as
a predictor of profile membership with `r3step()`; and as a covariate
estimated jointly with the profiles in a one-step model through
`profile_covariates`. The guide then shows how a covariate can affect an
indicator directly rather than through profile membership, a form of
differential item functioning that can otherwise be mistaken for a
difference between profiles, and concludes with staged estimation, in which
the group classes are estimated with the profiles held fixed through
`fit_staged()`.

## Data

`course_engagement` has one row per course enrolment: 1,422 enrolments from
106 students. `student` identifies the group, and five activity measures
(`browse`, `lectures`, `forum_read`, `forum_post`, `attendance`) are the
indicators. `previous_grade` is the standardized grade from the course before
each enrolment; it is not an indicator, so it can serve as an external
variable.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

## The measurement model

`multilpa()` fits the profiles without the external variable, with `vars`
for the indicators, `id` for the group, `n_profiles`, `n_group_classes`,
`n_starts` and `seed`. The within-profile covariances are estimated
(`covariance_model = "full"`), because the indicators are correlated within
profiles (see the
[multilevel latent profile analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lpa.html)
vignette).

```{r fit}
fit <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                         "attendance"),
                id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                covariance_model = "full",
                n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
fit
```

## Classification error

`get_results()` with `"classification_errors"` returns the
classification-error matrix, with `level` for the observations or the
groups.
Each row gives the probability of each assigned class for cases in a true
class; the three-step methods use it to correct for misclassification.

```{r errors}
get_results(fit, "classification_errors", level = "individuals")
```

Enrolments of the first profile are assigned to it with probability 0.982 and
those of the second with probability 0.968, so the corrections below are
small but not negligible.

## Class means of an external variable

`three_step()` estimates the mean of an external variable in each profile,
with `data` for the data frame and `outcome` for the variable. The default
method, BCH, corrects for classification error (Bolck et al., 2004; Bakk &
Vermunt, 2016); standard errors are clustered on groups.

```{r three-step}
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
```

Previous grades average 0.23 standard deviations above the mean before
enrolments of the first profile and 0.33 below it before enrolments of the
second. `contrast = "pairs"` returns each difference between profile means
with a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

```{r contrasts}
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           contrast = "pairs")
```

The difference is -0.57 standard deviations (95% interval -0.67 to -0.47).

Maximum likelihood is the other correction. With `method = "ml"`, the
assigned profile becomes an indicator of the true profile whose
classification errors are fixed at those of the measurement model, and the
external variable is normal within each profile, with its own variance. The
table adds that variance. When the variable is close to normal within
profiles, ML is usually more efficient than BCH (Vermunt, 2010), although with
classification as accurate as here the standard errors are nearly equal; when it is skewed, BCH
is the more robust choice.

```{r ml}
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           method = "ml")
```

ML gives nearly the same means (0.23 and -0.34), with variances of 0.93 and
0.91 within the profiles.

`method = "modal"` shows the effect of ignoring classification error: it
treats each case's most probable profile as known.

```{r modal}
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           method = "modal")
```

The modal means (0.22 and -0.32) are slightly closer together than the
corrected ones, the attenuation that classification error produces; with
classification as accurate as here, the difference is small.

## Predicting class membership

`r3step()` regresses profile membership on a covariate, with `data` for the
data frame and `covariates` for the predictors. It returns
multinomial logit coefficients, corrected for classification error.
`vcov_type = "robust"`, the default, clusters the standard errors on groups.

```{r r3step}
r3step(fit, data = course_engagement, covariates = "previous_grade",
       vcov_type = "robust")
```

A previous grade one standard deviation higher raises the log odds of the
first, more active profile against the second by 0.615 (95% interval 0.495
to 0.735), an odds ratio of about 1.85.

## One-step estimation

`multilpa()` with `profile_covariates` estimates the covariate together with
the profiles, as a predictor of profile membership.
`group_covariates` does the same for group-class membership and needs a
variable that is constant within groups. Covariates must have no missing
values; missing indicators are integrated out with `missing = "fiml"`.

```{r one-step}
one_step <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                     vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                              "forum_post", "attendance"),
                     id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                     covariance_model = "full",
                     profile_covariates = "previous_grade", n_starts = 3,
                     seed = 1)
one_step
```

`get_results()` with `"coefficients"` returns the membership coefficients,
and `parameter_inference()` the standard errors and intervals of every
parameter, beginning with the measurement means.

```{r coefficients}
get_results(one_step, "coefficients")
head(parameter_inference(one_step), 10)
```

The one-step coefficient of previous grade is 0.447, smaller than the
three-step coefficient, because it is conditional on the group class and the
profiles are estimated together with it.

## Direct effects on indicators

A covariate can also act on an indicator rather than on membership: students
with better previous grades may attend more within every profile. Left out
of the model, such an effect is read as a difference between the profiles
(differential item functioning). `multilpa()` with `direct_effects`
estimates it, one `"indicator ~ covariate"` term per effect. The
covariate shifts the indicator's mean by the same amount in every profile,
and the profile means are then the means at a covariate value of zero, here
the average standardized grade. Direct effects are estimated in a profile
model with a diagonal covariance structure (`EEI` or `VVI`), so the comparison
below uses the diagonal model with and without them.

```{r direct}
diagonal <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                     vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                              "forum_post", "attendance"),
                     id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                     n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
direct <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                   vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                            "forum_post", "attendance"),
                   id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                   direct_effects = c("attendance ~ previous_grade",
                                      "forum_post ~ previous_grade"),
                   n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
get_results(direct, "direct_effects")
compare_models(without = diagonal, direct = direct)
```

```{r direct-values, include = FALSE}
effects <- get_results(direct, "direct_effects")
effect_of <- function(name, column) with(subset(effects, indicator == name), get(column))
compared <- compare_models(without = diagonal, direct = direct)
bic_value <- function(name) with(subset(compared, model == name), bic_groups)
bic_of <- function(name) sprintf("%.1f", bic_value(name))
# The text below says BIC is lower without the effects; stop if that changes.
stopifnot(bic_value("without") < bic_value("direct"))
```

Attendance rises by `r round(effect_of("attendance", "estimate"), 3)` per
unit of previous grade within each profile (95% interval
`r round(effect_of("attendance", "conf_low"), 3)` to
`r round(effect_of("attendance", "conf_high"), 3)`), and forum posting by
`r round(effect_of("forum_post", "estimate"), 3)` (interval
`r round(effect_of("forum_post", "conf_low"), 3)` to
`r round(effect_of("forum_post", "conf_high"), 3)`). The effects are small
against the profile differences, and BIC is lower without them
(`r bic_of("without")` against `r bic_of("direct")`), so the profile differences on these indicators are not produced by direct
effects of previous grades.

## Staged estimation

`fit_staged()` holds the profiles fixed while the group classes are
estimated, with the arguments of `multilpa()` that define the profiles. It first fits the
profiles with one group class, then estimates the group classes with the
profile means and covariance matrices held fixed.

```{r staged}
staged <- fit_staged(course_engagement,
                     vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                              "forum_post", "attendance"),
                     id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                     covariance_model = "full",
                     n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
staged
```

`get_results()` with `"stages"` reports what each stage estimated.
`parameters` counts the parameters estimated at a stage, and
`parameters_with_measurement` adds those held fixed.

```{r stages}
get_results(staged, "stages")
```

The first stage estimates the 41 parameters of the profiles with one group
class; the second estimates 3 membership parameters with the profiles held
fixed.

## Reference

The calls below list other functions for external variables and fixed
parameters. Each comment states what the call returns.

```{r reference, eval = FALSE}
get_results(fit, "classification_errors", level = "groups")  # group-level errors
get_results(fit, "bch_weights", level = "individuals")       # BCH weights per case
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           method = "proportional")        # weighting by posterior probabilities
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           method = "ml", variance = "equal")  # ML with one shared variance
three_step(fit, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           vcov_type = "independent")      # standard errors without clustering
r3step(fit, data = course_engagement, covariates = "previous_grade",
       vcov_type = "observed")             # observed-information standard errors
measurement <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                        vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                                 "forum_post", "attendance"),
                        id = "student", n_profiles = 2,
                        n_group_classes = 1, covariance_model = "full",
                        seed = 1)  # a one-class measurement fit
fit_staged(course_engagement,
           vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                    "attendance"),
           id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
           covariance_model = "full",
           measurement = measurement)      # stage two from that fit
multilpa(course_engagement,
         vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                  "attendance"),
         id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
         covariance_model = "full",
         start = starting_values(fit, what = "measurement"),
         fixed = "variances")              # hold chosen parameters fixed
parameter_inference(staged)                # standard errors of the estimated stage
```

## Assumptions

- Three-step methods assume classification errors are independent of the
  external variable given the true class, and treat the error matrix as known.
- The ML correction also assumes the external variable is normal within each
  class; BCH does not.
- One-step coefficients are conditional on the group class and can change the
  profiles, so they need not equal the three-step coefficients.
- Staged estimation does not carry first-stage uncertainty into the second
  stage, and its likelihood is not the joint maximum.
- All associations are observational.
